boundary_tile.name: Boundary Tile
boundary_tile.description: One mosaic, four things it is willing to admit about its own seams, and the symmetry that decides which of the four is true. A 1.00 x 1.00 m field of 400 real tesserae - 0.043 m blocks in 0.007 m of grout, four palette colours at four heights - laid five tiles across from a hand-authored 4 x 4 motif, with the family's own boundary marks laid on top: a kerb at the rim, a frame and four posts round one unit cell, or a batten on every internal join. Three tokens in this corpus declare an axis called boundary and share one vocabulary exactly - none, edge, cell, lattice - and two of those tokens are ONE SCENE under two names, whose config block restates its own defaults. The code corrects three of the four glosses: edge is the outer rim of the WHOLE FIELD and says nothing about repeating, cell frames ONE unit once rather than each unit, and lattice deliberately EXCLUDES the rim so the two stay separate claims. What none of the three can do is read the symmetry, and that is the experiment: under plain the tile is the translational unit and lattice is exactly true, while under mirror the unit is two tiles on a diagonal and the same batten grid is wrong by a factor of two and by 45 degrees. The motif is invariant under a half-turn and its main diagonal, so mirror and rotate photograph identically at all four boundary values - two different wallpaper rules, one floor, four designed nulls. Nothing animates, nothing is random, nothing bakes on a worker thread.
dev_themes: a mark that asserts something the object cannot check
interactions: stand at boundary=none and walk the symmetry axis: under plain the diagonal ribbons run unbroken from edge to edge and you cannot find a single seam; under mirror they fold into chevrons and every fold is one. The axis has drawn nothing in either frame - that is the floor telling you about itself

put lattice/plain beside lattice/mirror: the same batten grid, computed from the same two numbers, over two floors whose real units are different. On the first it lands on every join; on the second it draws twice too many and points them the wrong way
compare mirror against rotate at any boundary value: the same photograph, to the byte. Two different wallpaper rules produced one floor, and no mark in the family's vocabulary can tell them apart

look for the cell frame's tile in the mirror and rotate frames: it is the centre tile, and it is the one tile in the field that all three symmetries leave alone. The value that holds up the unit holds up the one specimen carrying no information about the rule

note which value changes the outline. edge is the only mark standing at the rim, so it is the only one that alters the silhouette - and it is the only one of the four that was never about repeating in the first place
boundary_tile.capacity: SEE that a tiling's boundary marks are drawn from the tile grid, that the tile grid is only the pattern's unit when the symmetry says so, and that a family sharing one vocabulary across two scripts with opposite default symmetries is asserting two different things with the same four words

spatial_needs.footprint_note: THE FIELD IS THE FOOTPRINT AND IT IS DRAWN BEFORE EITHER AXIS IS CONSULTED: a 1.00 x 1.00 m bed with 400 tesserae on it, five tiles across. Nothing either axis does reaches past it. `symmetry` moves colours and heights inside a fixed grid and cannot move the grid; `boundary` adds marks whose outer faces land exactly on +-0.500 by the members' own e = side/2 - k/2. Only the HEIGHT moves, and only with `boundary`: none 0.064, lattice 0.089, edge 0.109, cell 0.175 - the four posts at 0.55 cell are the tallest thing here. So the world box is 1.000 x 0.175 x 1.000 in all twelve cells and the camera never moves. Orientation is `any` because the field is square and reads from every side; it is a floor piece and wants to be walked around rather than faced. layout=ladder stands all four boundaries in a row at 1.30 m pitch, about 4.9 m wide, and is a design view rather than a map placement.

measurements.source: computed_from_geometry in a Python replica built from the same constants; no Godot was run. The box is the bed plus the tallest mark: the bed spans x and z +-0.500 and is 0.018 thick, the tesserae top out at 0.064, the marks are seated on the tallest tessera at 0.065, and the cell posts run 0.110 above that to 0.175. Every one of the twelve variants shares the 1.000 x 1.000 footprint exactly; the y extent runs 0.064 at none to 0.175 at cell, which is why the union is 0.175 and why it is identical whichever cell is measured.

dna.default: boundary=none, symmetry=plain. `none` is the family's unanimous default and the count is THREE OF THREE: pattern_maker_station.gd:81 and vr_tile_editor.gd:52 both declare `var boundary: String = "none"`, and the third token inherits it because vr_tile_editor_mirror is the same scene. No map in the corpus sets it to anything else. `plain` IS THIS BENCH'S CHOICE AND THE FAMILY HAS NO DEFAULT TO INHERIT, which is itself the finding: pattern_maker_station starts at _group_index 0 = P1, pure translation, while vr_tile_editor ships repeat_mode = 3 = MIRROR_XY. The two scripts sharing one boundary vocabulary ship OPPOSITE symmetries. `plain` is taken because it is RepeatMode.SIMPLE, the enum's zero, and because it is the one floor on which the family's boundary words are all true - so the default cell is the axis's best case, and every departure from it is a departure toward being wrong.
dna.note:
WHAT THE VALUES MEAN, where each word came from, and which of them can be WRONG.

THE FAMILY FIRST, and it is a census before it is an argument. Three registry tokens declare an axis called `boundary` and all three carry ONE vocabulary, word for word and in the same order: none | edge | cell | lattice. THE THREE TOKENS ARE TWO SCRIPTS. pattern_maker_station.tscn runs pattern_maker_station.gd; vr_tile_editor.tscn runs vr_tile_editor.gd; and `vr_tile_editor_mirror` POINTS AT THE SAME .tscn as `vr_tile_editor` - res://commons/primitives/arrays/vr_tile_editor.tscn, checked in arrays.json at both entries. One scene, two names, the corpus's most common hidden family found again. And it goes one step past the usual case: the mirror token carries a `config` block of {tile_size: 4, repeat_mode: 3} while the shared script's own export defaults are tile_size = 4 and repeat_mode = 3, so THE CONFIG RESTATES THE DEFAULTS AND CHANGES NOTHING. The two names are not two objects and they are not even two configurations.

THE DEFAULT IS UNANIMOUS AND THE COUNT IS THREE OF THREE. Both scripts declare `@export_enum("none", "edge", "cell", "lattice") var boundary: String = "none"` - pattern_maker_station.gd:81 and vr_tile_editor.gd:52 - and the third token inherits it from the shared scene. No map anywhere sets it.

THREE OF THE BRIEF'S FOUR GLOSSES WERE WRONG AND THE CODE SAYS SO PLAINLY. The brief read the axis as a ladder of how much modularity the pattern admits: none hides it, edge marks the tile border, cell marks each unit inside the tile, lattice marks the whole grid. What the two `_build_boundary` implementations actually draw is this:

  none      NOTHING. `if boundary == "none": return` before a root node exists, in both files. The floor arrives seamless and says nothing about itself, which is what a finished mosaic wants you to believe. DRAWN AREA 0.

  edge      A KERB ROUND THE OUTER RIM OF THE WHOLE FIELD - not the tile border. `_boundary_kerb` builds four bars of the FULL side length at e = side/2 - k/2, k = 0.30 cell wide and t = 0.22 cell tall, and both files' own comments say what it means: the floor "admits it is a made object with an end, and still says nothing about repeating". So `edge` is not on the modularity question at all. It is the only value answering "where does this object stop?", and here it is the only value that changes the SILHOUETTE, because it is the only one standing at the outline. Drawn: 0.060 x 0.044 m section, 0.2256 m2 = 22.56 percent of the field, top at y 0.109.

  cell      ONE unit cell framed and posted, ONCE, among its copies - not each unit inside a tile. `_boundary_cell` frames a single tile with four battens (b = 0.12 cell, t = 0.25 cell) and stands four posts at its corners (0.18 cell square, 0.55 cell tall). The index is `reps / 2` with a half-cell offset, which the members added so an EVEN repeat count would not put the frame on a join; at REPS = 5 that same arithmetic returns 2 and the frame lands dead centre. Drawn: 0.0267 m2 = 2.67 percent of the field, the smallest mark in the sheet, top at y 0.175 - the tallest thing here, and the posts are why.

  lattice   A BATTEN ON EVERY INTERNAL UNIT BOUNDARY, and the brief's question - does lattice include edge? - is answered NO, deliberately, in both files. `for i in range(1, reps)` excludes the rim, and both comments give the reason: "The outer edge is left to `edge`, so the two values stay separate claims". Drawn: b = 0.10 cell, t = 0.12 cell, 0.1536 m2 = 15.36 percent, top at y 0.089. lattice and edge are DISJOINT sets of marks, and no boundary value is a subset of another except by position: cell's four battens sit ON four of lattice's lines, but wider (0.024 against 0.020), taller (0.050 against 0.024) and with four posts lattice has not got.

SO THE AXIS IS NOT ONE LADDER. It is: no claim / a claim about the END / a claim about the UNIT, once / a claim about the unit, EVERYWHERE. And the claim about the unit is the one that can be FALSE, which is what the second axis is for.

SYMMETRY, three values, taken verbatim from pattern_tile_puzzle.gd's `_get_tiled_color` - the function both members' carpets are ultimately drawn from, ten repeat modes deep, of which this bench sweeps three.

  plain    RepeatMode.SIMPLE (:1252). `tx = px % n; ty = py % n`. Pure translation. The tile IS the translational unit cell, so on this floor `lattice` is exactly true and `cell` frames a real unit. This is pattern_maker_station's shipped condition: its default _group_index is 0 and GROUP_ORDER[0] is P1.

  mirror   RepeatMode.MIRROR_XY (:1270), the kaleidoscope, AND THE OPERATION vr_tile_editor_mirror IS NAMED FOR: `if tile_x % 2 == 1: tx = n - 1 - tx`, and the same in y. Every seam becomes a reflection axis. This is vr_tile_editor's shipped condition - repeat_mode = 3 at vr_tile_editor.gd:23. WHICH MEANS THE FAMILY'S TWO SCRIPTS SHIP OPPOSITE SYMMETRIES UNDER ONE SHARED BOUNDARY VOCABULARY.

  rotate   RepeatMode.ROTATE_90 (:1280), and the idiosyncrasy is the source's, not this bench's: the turn count is `(px / n + py / n) % 4`, the SUM of the tile indices, so quarter-turns cascade along the anti-diagonal instead of filling a 2 x 2 block.

WHAT THE CROSSING SHOWS, and it is the thesis. `_build_boundary` in BOTH members is computed from the field size and the repeat count ALONE. Neither reads the symmetry; neither can. So the marks are bit-identical under all three values of `symmetry`, and the question is whether they are still TRUE. Under `plain` the translational lattice is generated by (4, 0) and (0, 4) tesserae - one tile - so lattice's battens land on every real join and nowhere else. Under `mirror` the field's translational lattice is generated by (4, 4) and (4, -4): the unit cell contains TWO tiles and it is DIAGONAL. lattice then draws twice too many battens in each direction and points them the wrong way, and `cell`'s frame is no longer a translational unit cell at all - it is the fundamental domain of a reflection group, a different object wearing the same word. The vocabulary is true on exactly one of the two floors its own two scripts ship.

THE MOTIF IS THE INSTRUMENT AND IT WAS CHOSEN FOR TWO PROPERTIES. (1) It is invariant under a half-turn and under its main diagonal, and NOT under a horizontal or vertical mirror - the four values are 3 on the diagonal, 1 beside it, 0 next, 2 in the off corners. Under those two invariances MIRROR_XY and ROTATE_90 produce the SAME FIELD, tessera for tessera: wherever mirror applies a flip, rotate applies a quarter-turn, and the half-turn plus the diagonal carry one onto the other. Verified cell by cell in a Python replica for all 25 tiles - 400 of 400 identical. (2) It is a graded diagonal ribbon, so under `plain` the ribbons run UNBROKEN across the whole field and there is no visible seam anywhere, while under `mirror` they fold into chevrons and every fold is a seam. 192 of 400 tesserae change between plain and mirror.

WHICH SHARPENS THE BRIEF'S CLAIM AND ALSO CORRECTS IT. The brief said that at `none` a viewer cannot locate the repeat and at `lattice` they cannot avoid it. Half true. At `none` under `plain` the repeat is genuinely unlocatable - worse than unlocatable, the eye reads a diagonal period of ONE tessera where the true period is four, so the floor actively misleads. But at `none` under `mirror` the chevrons announce the unit without any help from the axis, and there `lattice` is not revelation but redundancy - and wrong redundancy, at that. THE AXIS IS NOT ABOUT VISIBILITY. It is about ASSERTION: whether the object says the thing, and whether the thing it says is so.

RELIEF, NOT TEXTURE, and the reason is measurement rather than taste. Both members render their carpet as an ImageTexture on a QuadMesh - a picture of a mosaic - which is also part of why the interaction harness cannot see either of them move. Here every tessera is a box, 400 of them at 0.043 m across with 0.007 m of grout, and the height carries the pattern a SECOND time: 0.008 / 0.028 / 0.016 / 0.046 m for cream / red / navy / gold. That is the colour-trap guard. The critic measures luminance by default, and red (Rec.709 0.324) and navy (0.247) sit within 0.077 of each other - the twin condition exactly. They differ by 0.012 m of height here, so the shading separates them whatever the critic looks at. The palette itself is the family's, verbatim: PatternMakerStation.PALETTE[0..3] at pattern_maker_station.gd:30-33, the Italian textile set PatternTilePuzzle and ArrayCarpet also carry. The marks' stone is verbatim too - albedo (0.87, 0.85, 0.79), roughness 0.55, metallic 0.05, identical in both files at pattern_maker_station.gd:715 and vr_tile_editor.gd:432.

THE EXTENTS, because they are the free half of this design. The field is 1.00 x 1.00 m in every one of the twelve cells and nothing reaches past it: the kerb's outer face lands exactly on +-0.500 by the members' own e = side/2 - k/2. Only the height moves - none 0.064, lattice 0.089, edge 0.109, cell 0.175 - and `symmetry` never moves anything at all, because it changes colours and heights inside a fixed grid. Union AABB 1.000 x 0.175 x 1.000, diagonal 1.425 m, identical in all twelve, so the camera never moves.

THE THESIS SOMEONE COULD DISAGREE WITH: a pattern's `boundary` marks are drawn from the tile grid, and the tile grid is not the pattern's unit unless the symmetry says so - so three of the family's four values are assertions that can be false, and the family has no way to check them. THE DISAGREEMENT AVAILABLE, and it is fair: a reader can say that `lattice` never claimed to be a translational unit cell, only to show the grid the editor edits on, in which case it is true by definition and this whole bench is answering a question nobody asked. The answer is that both members' own comments call it "the repeat made countable" and "the floor re-read as the array it is" - a claim about the FLOOR, not about the editor - and that the two scripts ship opposite symmetries, so under the family's own defaults the same four words describe two different floors one room apart.

predicted_degeneracy.pair: none against cell, in the mirror symmetry
predicted_degeneracy.arithmetic:
Rasterised BEFORE ANY CAPTURE in the critic's own currency: the geometry rebuilt in Python from the same constants (same motif, same three symmetry branches transcribed from _get_tiled_color, same mark coefficients), projected through capture_config_sweep's camera (FOV 34, PAD 1.9, yaw 0.62, pitch -0.26, 760 x 760, framing 0.64 on the union AABB of all twelve variants, which is 1.000 x 0.175 x 1.000 and therefore identical in every cell), z-buffered with the default rig unchanged - key at (-42, -35) energy 1.25, fill at (-20, 130) energy 0.45, ambient (0.62, 0.65, 0.72) at 0.55, background (0.055, 0.055, 0.070), FILMIC, sRGB out - then run through artifact_dna_critic's pipeline unchanged: subject bbox from pixel (3,3), crop to the union of the two frames' subject boxes, neutralise each frame's own corner, grey, resize 160 x 160, mean of the hottest 5 percent.

THE CONTEXT IS THE `mirror` SYMMETRY AND THE RANKING IS COMPUTED INSIDE IT. All six boundary pairs, focus percent: none-cell 26.00, cell-lattice 51.89, none-lattice 53.54, edge-lattice 86.83, edge-cell 86.84, none-edge 86.84.

IT IS A CLUSTER OF TWO CONTEXTS, NOT ONE, AND THAT IS SAID IN ADVANCE. none against cell in `rotate` is THE SAME NUMBER TO THE BYTE, because mirror and rotate are the same frame to the byte - which is the designed null. In `plain` the same pair reads 28.02, about 8 percent higher; the difference is not the marks (identical) and not the tile they frame (the centre tile is fixed by all three symmetries, verified), it is the FOUR NEIGHBOURING tiles the battens overhang by 0.012 m, which are not fixed.

WHY THAT PAIR. `cell` is the smallest mark in the family - 0.0267 m2 against lattice's 0.1536 and edge's 0.2256 - so it changes the least. Its screen footprint is roughly 0.061 m2 of a 2.98 m2 frame, about 2.0 percent, while the critic's hottest-5-percent window over the cropped subject box is about 0.036 m2. The window therefore fills entirely with mark pixels and the number is set by CONTRAST, not by area: stone at albedo luma 0.850 replacing a field whose mean is 0.437 once the 26 percent grout share is counted, and the hottest pixels are stone over navy (0.247) and stone over grout (0.200), giving a mean separation near 66 of 255 = 26 percent. 26.00.

THIS PREDICTION CANNOT UNDER-READ BY THE CORPUS'S USUAL FACTOR, and that is worth saying because every prior prediction here under-read by 1.5x to 6.7x. There is no room: 26.00 percent is 66 grey levels, the three edge pairs already sit at 86.8, and the metric caps at 100. What this pair CAN do is come in low, and that is the thing to watch. IF THE SWEEP COMES BACK BELOW 26.00 ON THE NAMED PAIR, STOP AND INVESTIGATE THE HARNESS BEFORE THE DESIGN: (a) tools/check_dna_declarations.py - a value the code cannot reach falls back to the default and prints identical tiles; (b) _rejects.json - all three exports are String enums and Object.set() on a typed property of the wrong type is refused in SILENCE; (c) whether the sheet was captured with --max=12, because at build_dna_gallery's default cap of 9 the 4 x 3 cross product is trimmed from the tail of the LATER axis and `symmetry` collapses to [plain, mirror], which deletes every one of the four designed nulls and half the argument.

THE RISK THAT IS NOT IN THE REGISTERED NUMBER: the three pairs that cross `edge` all land within 0.02 of each other at 86.8, which is not three measurements but one - the hottest 5 percent is entirely kerb-against-background in every one of them, because `edge` is the only value that breaks the silhouette. If those three come back spread out instead of clustered, the kerb is not standing where this replica put it, and the first thing to check is whether the marks were seated on the bed instead of on the tallest tessera.

designed_nulls.why: IDENTICAL BY CONSTRUCTION AND IT IS THE THESIS. The motif is invariant under a half-turn and under its main diagonal, and under those two conditions MIRROR_XY and ROTATE_90 land on the same tessera of the motif at every one of the 25 tiles: where mirror flips (ti odd, tj even) the code reads M[ty][n-1-tx], where rotate turns once it reads M[tx][n-1-ty], and the diagonal invariance carries one onto the other while the half-turn carries the remaining cases. Verified tile by tile on the replica - 400 of 400 tesserae equal - and measured at 0.0000 percent focus / 0.0000 percent frame. TWO DIFFERENT WALLPAPER RULES, ONE PHOTOGRAPH. This is the null the boundary axis is blind to and the reason it can be wrong: the floor does not record which rule made it. Anything above 0.5 percent is render noise; anything above 2 percent means the motif in the shipped file is not the motif in this note.

The same null with the kerb standing. Registered separately because the marks are the loudest thing in the frame at this value - 22.56 percent of the field - and if `boundary` were reaching the pattern anywhere, the value that covers the most of it is where a leak would show first. The kerb geometry is a function of side and reps only, in this file exactly as in both members', so it is the same four bars in both frames.

The same null with the frame and posts standing, and this one carries a second fact worth having: the tile `cell` frames is the CENTRE tile (ti = tj = 2), which mirror leaves alone because both indices are even and rotate leaves alone because (2 + 2) % 4 = 0. So the one tile the family holds up as "the unit" is a tile on which all three symmetries agree - it cannot tell you which rule made the floor even in principle. The posts also make this the tallest variant (0.175 m), so it is the pair where a framing or AABB fault would show as a non-zero.

The same null with the full batten grid standing, and the one that closes the set. All four must be 0.00 together; three zeros and one non-zero is arithmetically impossible for identical images and would be a fact about the harness rather than about the artifact - most likely an unsettled first tile, which is why the critic neutralises each frame's own corner. It is also the pair where the argument is at its sharpest: the identical batten grid is TRUE of neither floor, since both mirror and rotate have a two-tile diagonal unit, and the two frames cannot be told apart.

dna.designed_nulls_why: FOUR NULLS, ONE FACT, AND IT IS THE ARGUMENT. mirror and rotate are two different wallpaper rules - a reflection group and a rotation group - and on this motif they produce the same floor tessera for tessera, because the motif is invariant under a half-turn and under its main diagonal. So the four nulls say: THE FLOOR DOES NOT RECORD WHICH RULE MADE IT. And the boundary marks, which are computed from the field size and the repeat count alone in both members, cannot record it either - they are the same battens in both frames. That is why `lattice` can be false: it asserts a unit, the unit is a property of the rule, and neither the floor nor the mark carries the rule. The tempting fifth null is `cell` against `none` in mirror, where the framed tile is the symmetry-invariant centre tile, and it is deliberately NOT a null: the marks are there, and that 26.00 percent is the pre-registered closest pair. If any of the four zeros comes back above 2 percent, nothing else in this sheet can be believed - and the first place to look is the motif, because a single transcription slip in the 4 x 4 breaks the half-turn or the diagonal and takes all four with it.
dna.fixture_why: The bench can stand all four boundaries in a row (layout=ladder, 1.30 m pitch, about 4.9 m wide) but the SWEEP must see one at a time: capture_config_sweep unions the AABB across a spec's variants, so a four-wide row in the same spec would frame every single cell against nearly five metres and photograph a 20 mm batten as a hairline - which is precisely lesson (e), a mark falling under the critic's blank floor. layout is an export and not an axis, and it ships at single, so the fixture is a belt over braces. WHAT IS NOT FIXTURED, AND WHY NOTHING NEEDS TO BE: there is no clock and no random number here. All 400 tesserae and every mark are built synchronously inside _ready from arithmetic on ten constants and a hand-authored 4 x 4 - no _process, no Timer, no randf, no FastNoiseLite, and deliberately no ImageTexture, which is how both members build their carpets and which would put the whole pattern behind a texture upload. That matters because the sources are not so quiet: pattern_maker_station runs a _process every frame polling for touch-paint, and its apply_grid_config stores nine keys that are never read again because the grid calls it AFTER _ready has already built from the export defaults - the file says so in its own comment at :689.
dna.kin: The three sources are the kin and two of them are one file. pattern_maker_station is an upright panel and a 4 m carpet driven by a GPU wallpaper shader across all 17 groups, whose truth line is that structure emerges from constraint applied to the almost-nothing; vr_tile_editor is a tilted editing board at desk height over a 3 m carpet, whose truth line is that the editing board is the source code and the carpet is the running program. Both make the same move - a small domain in the hands, an unbounded field underfoot - and both hand the actual tiling to PatternTilePuzzle. WHY THE INTERACTION HARNESS FOUND BOTH vr_tile_editor NAMES INERT, and the code explains it exactly: vr_tile_editor declares no controls of its own. `_find_controllers` awaits a process frame and then walks the scene tree for nodes named LeftController / RightController / LeftHand / RightHand and connects `button_pressed` to them - so in a harness with no XR rig, nothing is found and every listener count is zero by construction, which is what "every control dangling" means. Everything else is FORWARDED: `_on_button_pressed` and the whole keyboard fallback call `_puzzle.handle_vr_button`, so the controls belong to a child scene the harness was not measuring. And even when a cell does change, the result is an ImageTexture rebuilt pixel by pixel and assigned to `albedo_texture` - the carpet's GEOMETRY never moves, so a harness watching transforms sees a fired control and a still world. That is not a dead artifact; it is three separate ways for a live one to photograph dead, and it is the same disease as the INERT verdicts this programme keeps having to retract. This bench is built the opposite way on purpose: the pattern is 400 boxes, so a change in the pattern is a change in the geometry. ON THE VALUE SIDE this is the corpus's cleanest shared vocabulary - four words, three tokens, two scripts, no disagreement anywhere, and the two `_build_boundary` implementations agree to the last coefficient (0.30, 0.22 / 0.12, 0.25, 0.18, 0.55 / 0.10, 0.12). Which is exactly why the interesting question is not whether they mean the same thing but whether the thing they mean is true.
declines: THE BRIEF'S GLOSS OF `edge`, corrected from the code and it is the biggest change. The brief said edge marks the tile border. It does not: `_boundary_kerb` builds four bars of the FULL side length round the outer rim of the whole field, and both members' own headers say it admits the floor is a made object with an end "and still says nothing about repeating". So `edge` is not a point on the modularity ladder at all - it answers a different question, where the object stops, and it is the only value that does. The bench is built the same way either reading, but the note now says which is true, and the axis is described as two questions rather than one ladder.

THE BRIEF'S GLOSS OF `cell`, corrected the same way. The brief said cell marks each unit inside the tile. `_boundary_cell` frames exactly ONE unit cell, once, at the index reps / 2 with a half-cell offset - a single specimen among its copies, which is a different claim and a weaker one. Both members' own headers use the word "once".

THE BRIEF'S QUESTION ABOUT WHETHER `lattice` INCLUDES `edge`, answered against the guess: NO, and deliberately. `for i in range(1, reps)` excludes the rim in both files, and both comments give the same reason - "the outer edge is left to `edge`, so the two values stay separate claims". There is therefore no subset null available between any two boundary values, which is why the designed nulls in this sheet all live on the `symmetry` axis instead.

THE BRIEF'S PROPOSED CHECK - that `edge` should be invisible under `mirror` where two reflected tiles meet seamlessly and visible under `plain` where they do not. NOT CONSTRUCTIBLE, because the family's `edge` is the rim of the whole carpet and never touches a tile seam. The interaction the family never crosses is real, but it is `lattice` against `symmetry`, not `edge`: lattice draws the tile grid, and the tile grid is the translational unit under plain and is not under mirror. That substitution is the whole second axis.

THE 17 WALLPAPER GROUPS. pattern_maker_station's critical parameter is `wallpaper_group` and it cycles all seventeen through WallpaperGroups.get_symmetric_color; PatternTilePuzzle carries them too, alongside its ten legacy repeat modes. Three of seventeen is the whole sweep here, and the three chosen are the legacy modes rather than the group table, because the legacy branch is arithmetic this file can transcribe line for line and audit, while get_symmetric_color is a second file's interpretation of a crystallographic table. A bench that swept P1 / PMM / P4 would be measuring that table's fidelity, which is a different and worthwhile pass.

BRICK_X, BRICK_Y, HERRINGBONE and DIAMOND from the same enum. All four are real family values and all four would bite. They are declined because they OFFSET rather than re-orient - BRICK_X shifts alternate rows by half a tile - and an offset changes where the tile boundaries ARE, which would make `lattice` misaligned rather than merely wrong about the unit. That is a third failure mode and it deserves its own sheet rather than a quarter of this one.

THE MEMBERS' TEN AND EIGHT REPEATS, REDUCED TO FIVE, and this is a real deviation with a number attached. Both members draw a cell about 0.4 m across; at 1 m and ten repeats the cell would be 0.1 m and the family's cell-relative mark arithmetic would put `cell`'s frame at 0.0068 m2 - 0.68 percent of the field, roughly 0.7 percent of frame, close enough to the critic's blank floor (~0.2 percent) to make an honest mark read as a hairline. At five repeats the marks keep the members' exact proportions AGAINST THE CELL and come out twice as heavy against the FIELD. Five is also odd, which is why `cell` lands dead centre where the members' even counts deliberately dodge off-centre.

THE CARPET AS A TEXTURE. Both members build theirs as an ImageTexture on a QuadMesh, computed pixel by pixel. Reproducing that would have been more faithful and was declined for two reasons: a boundary mark laid ON a floor needs a floor with a surface to rest on, and a texture upload is exactly the class of thing that can photograph unbaked in a headless sweep - the stale-shader fault in another costume. 400 boxes cost 4800 triangles and are built synchronously. It also lets the height ladder carry the pattern a second time, which is what keeps red and navy off the greyscale-twin line.

ANIMATION, AND EVERY RATE. Neither member animates its boundary and neither has a rate to sweep; pattern_maker_station's _process only polls for touch-paint. The same refusal holds here and it is not a close call - a boundary mark is a static assertion, and a still is the correct and only instrument for it.

THE MOSAIC'S WEAR. pattern_maker_station carries six aging exports - wear, dust, fade, crack, stain, chip - all of them GPU-shader-only and all of them stored-and-never-read from a map token. They are not built here. They are surface, this axis is about assertion, and every one of them would move the pattern's luminance and confound the mark against the field it is drawn on.

A THIRD AXIS FROM THE MEMBERS. pattern_maker_station's other declared question is the wallpaper group; vr_tile_editor's is carpet_repeats, which its own @identity calls the critical parameter. carpet_repeats is the tempting one and it is exactly the wrong one to cross with `boundary`, because every boundary mark's SIZE is computed from the cell, so the two axes would move the same pixels and neither could be attributed.
dna.sweep_note: THE FULL SHEET NEEDS --max=12 AND THE COST OF GETTING IT WRONG IS ALL FOUR NULLS. `boundary` is declared first and is never trimmed; `symmetry` is second, and build_dna_gallery trims the LATER axis from the tail until the cross product fits its cap. At the default --max=9 the 4 x 3 sheet renders as 4 x 2 = plain and mirror only, which deletes `rotate` and with it every one of the four designed nulls - the entire mirror-equals-rotate finding - and leaves a finished-looking sheet of eight tiles that still shows the boundary axis biting and cannot be wrong about anything. Only 12 carries the experiment.
